definition: Overview: Brown v. Board of Education (Brown I), 347 U.S. 483 (1954) was a landmark U.S. Supreme Court decision that struck down the “Separate but Equal” doctrine and outlawed the ongoing segregation in public schools. The Court ruled that laws mandating and enforcing racial segregation in public schools were unconstitutional, even if the segregated schools were “separate but equal” in standards. The Supreme Court’s decision was unanimous and held that "separate educational facilities are inherently unequal," and hence a violation of the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution. Nonetheless, since the ruling did not list or specify a specific method or timeline for ending racial segregation in schools, the Court's ruling in Brown v. Board of Education (Brown II), 349 U.S. 294 (1955) demanded states to desegregate “with all deliberate speed.” Background: The events relevant to this specific case first occurred in 1951, when a public school district in Topeka, Kansas refused to let Oliver Brown’s daughter enroll at the nearest school to their home and instead required her to enroll at a school further away. Oliver Brown and his daughter were Black. The Brown family, along with twelve other local Black families in similar circumstances, filed a class action lawsuit in federal court against the Topeka Board of Education, arguing that the segregation policy of forcing Black students to attend separate schools was unconstitutional. However, the U.S. District Court for the District of Kansas ruled against the Browns, justifying their decision on judicial precedent of the Supreme Court's 1896 decision in Plessy v. Ferguson, 163 U.S. 537 (1896), which ruled that racial segregation did not violate the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause as long as the facilities and situations were equal, hence the doctrine known as "separate but equal." After this decision from the District Court in Kansas, the Browns, who were represented by the then NAACP Chief Counsel Thurgood Marshall, appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court.
